blocks.text:
Heather Smith
Chief Financial Officer
Carter and Sons
Dear Ms. Smith,

This letter sets out the terms on which Saltmarsh Environmental Partners will carry out the habitat restoration monitoring we discussed for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}, and it asks you to countersign so that a signed copy is in the file before the first field visit. I have kept the language plain. The clauses toward the end read as standard terms because they are, and each is here because it has earned a place on work of this kind.

The restoration area you established under your permit has to be monitored on the schedule the permit sets, and measured against the success criteria the permit names. This engagement covers one monitoring season of that program. It includes the field data collection, the analysis of what we find, and a written monitoring report addressed to the agency reviewer who will read it. We will monitor the vegetation, the hydrology, and the presence of invasive species across the restoration area, at the sample plots and along the fixed transects the monitoring plan lays out.

Our method follows the monitoring plan approved for the site. We hold to it from one visit to the next, so this season's data read against the seasons before and after it. Vegetation is recorded along the fixed transects and in the sample plots, by species and by cover. Hydrology is read at the established gauges. Photographs are taken from the same photo stations and on the same headings, so the panels line up over the years. Every observation is tied to its plot, its station, and the date it was made. William Schwartz runs the field visits and keeps the field record, and on a monitoring program that record is as much a deliverable as the numbers are.

The season's data are compiled into a workbook, each figure carried back to the plot and the date behind it. I check the totals in that workbook against the field record myself before the report is drafted. James Henderson writes the monitoring report from the checked data. It states what was measured, where, and on what date, and it compares the season's results against the permit's success criteria without reaching past what the data support. Where a criterion has not been met, the report says so and notes what the record shows. We do not present a shortfall as a success, and we do not read more into one good season than the data will bear.

You will have three things from the season: the monitoring report, the data workbook that stands behind it, and the field record for every visit. The report is the document that goes to the agency. The workbook and the field record are what let anyone, including a reviewer years from now, check the report against what was actually done on the ground. We keep copies of all three, and all three are yours.

You will deal mostly with two of our people. William Schwartz, our Field Technician, runs the monitoring visits, the transects, and the photo stations, and works to the tide and the season rather than the office calendar. James Henderson, our Environmental Scientist, handles the desk work and writes the monitoring report for the agency. I sign what leaves this office and review the workbook before anything is submitted, so my name is on the report alongside theirs.

Because the estuary is tidal, the visits are planned around the water and the season, not to fixed dates, so that each reading is clean and comparable with the last. That can move a visit by a day or two. When it does, William will let your site contact know in advance. It changes neither the fee nor the method, which hold from the first visit to the last.

The fee for this season's monitoring is a fixed {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}. It covers the field collection, the data workbook, the analysis, and the monitoring report as described above. It does not cover work outside that scope. If the site turns up something that calls for more than this letter describes, I will tell you before we do it and not after. We are prepared to begin on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}, subject to site access and to conditions on the estuary.
Fees and Payment

The fixed fee is invoiced in two parts: half when the work commences and the balance on delivery of the monitoring report. Invoices are due within thirty days. Anything you ask us to add beyond the scope above is billed at cost, and only after you have approved it in writing.
Term and Termination

The engagement runs from commencement until the monitoring report is delivered and accepted. Either of us may end it on fifteen days' written notice. If you end it partway through, you owe us for the fieldwork completed and for any commitments already made to that point, and we will hand over the field record and the data we hold so that the season's work is not lost.
Confidentiality

We treat your site information, your business information, and the terms of this engagement as confidential, and we do not discuss them outside the firm without your consent. The monitoring report is the exception the permit requires, since it is submitted to the agency, along with any disclosure the law compels. Where we are required to disclose, we will tell you what is going and to whom, so far as we are allowed to.
Limitation of Liability

Our findings rest on the conditions present at the sample plots on the days they were monitored, and a restoration area changes from season to season and across its own ground. Our liability for this engagement is limited to the amount of the fee, and we are not responsible for decisions made on the basis of the report beyond what its data support. That limit reflects what one season of monitoring can establish, and no more.
Governing Law
This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which the site sits, and any dispute under it will be settled there.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign below and return one copy to me for the file, keeping the other for yours. If anything reads differently from what we discussed, call me before you sign and we will settle it first. I am glad to be taking this on, and I expect the record this season produces to stand up to the reading the agency will give it.

To: James Henderson, Environmental Scientist
From: William Schwartz, Field Technician
Re: Carter and Sons restoration monitoring, start-up

This memo starts the monitoring season for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. The engagement is one season of the restoration monitoring the site's permit requires. Our job is plain. Measure the site on the plan's method, check it against the permit's success criteria, and produce the monitoring report the agency will read.

Three things come out of the season. The monitoring report, the data workbook behind it, and the field record for every visit. The report goes to the agency. The other two are what let anyone check it.

This is one season of a multi-season monitoring requirement. Each season has to read against the others. So we hold the method fixed and keep the stations where the plan puts them, from the first visit to the last.

The report is written for an agency reviewer, not for us. Someone may open it years from now with no one left to ask what a note meant. So we write the record so it reads without us, and we keep it plain.
The season's work, by piece

items: Vegetation. Record species and cover along the fixed transects and in the sample plots. Same transects, same plots, same method the plan sets.
Hydrology. Read the established gauges on each visit. Log the reading, the station, and the date.
Photo stations. Shoot each station from the same point and the same heading, so the panels line up against prior years.
Invasive species. Note presence and extent across the area. Flag anything that has spread since the last record.
Field record. Tie every observation to its plot, its station, and its date. Notes go into the workbook on the day, not at month end.
Access and safety. Confirm the crossing to the far plots and the on-site contact before each visit.
Report. James Henderson drafts the monitoring report from the checked data. It states what was measured, where, and when, and compares against the success criteria.

blocks.text: Our contact at Carter and Sons is Heather Smith, their Chief Financial Officer. She handles site access and scheduling on their end. If a visit has to move for the tide or the weather, she is the one to tell, and to tell early.
The visits are planned to the season and the tide, not to a fixed calendar. That can move a day here or there. It does not change the stations, the method, or what we deliver.

One thing on the field record. Enter the notes the day of the visit, while the site is fresh, and bring me anything that looks off on site instead of working around it. Two of the plots sit across the channel and are only safe to reach on the right water. Nobody works a station that is not safe to work, and a plot missed for the tide is caught on the next suitable window.

On a visit day the split is simple. I run the stations and the record. James takes the desk side and the write-up. The workbook totals are checked before anything is submitted, so a figure that leaves the office is one someone has stood behind.
Before the first visit

Field work begins on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}. Before then, I want the transect and plot list confirmed against the monitoring plan, the gauges and photo stations located and checked, and the field kit gone over. James and I will walk the visit order this week.
The single next step is the site walk. James and I confirm the station order and the access points this week, so the first day on site is spent measuring and not deciding. — William Schwartz
Minutes: Habitat Restoration Monitoring, Working Session

These minutes record a working session on the habitat restoration monitoring for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. The session reviewed the first monitoring visit of the season, settled a question of site access, and set the next visit. The notes follow the order of the discussion, and each action is recorded with an owner so that nothing agreed here is left without a name against it.
Present:

items: William Schwartz, Field Technician, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
James Henderson, Environmental Scientist, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Heather Smith, Chief Financial Officer, Carter and Sons

blocks.text: First visit. The first monitoring visit was completed at the fixed transects and the sample plots. Vegetation was recorded by species and cover, the gauges were read, and the photo stations were shot on their established headings. Conditions on the day were suitable, and nothing about the visit departed from the plan.

Field record. William Schwartz confirmed that the field notebook and the station log are current through the first visit, with each observation tied to its plot and its date. The record is being kept in the standard format, so that this season and the next will read the same way side by side.

Early observations. It is early, and I would caution against reading a single visit as a trend. The planted stock appears to be establishing across most of the area, though two plots are thinner than the others. We will note both and watch them. A season's data, and not one visit, will show whether either is a concern.

Invasive species. A stand of an invasive species was noted along the upland edge. Its extent was measured and photographed. Whether it has advanced since the prior record is a question the file will answer, and William Schwartz will check the earlier notes against what we saw.

Site access. Access to the far side of the restoration area has been uncertain at high water. Heather Smith agreed to arrange a reliable crossing for the field crew and a point of contact on site, so that a visit is not lost to the tide.

Data workbook. The workbook has been set up with the full station list and the plot identifiers already in place, so that each visit's readings can be entered against them on the day. The totals will be reconciled against the field record before any figure is shared outside the firm.

The report. I noted that the monitoring report will be drafted once the season's visits are complete and the workbook has been checked. It will compare the results against the permit's success criteria, and it will not characterize the site on partial data.

Next visit. We agreed to set the next visit to the season's window and the tide rather than to a fixed date, on the same stations and by the same method, so the two visits remain directly comparable. That also leaves the crew room if the water does not cooperate on the planned day.

rows: Keep the field record current for each visit
Check the earlier notes against the invasive stand recorded this visit
Arrange reliable site access and an on-site contact
Schedule the next visit to the season's window

blocks.text: The single next step is the next monitoring visit. Once Heather Smith confirms access and the window is set, William Schwartz and I will run it on the same transects and by the same method as the first.
Status Report: Habitat Restoration Monitoring

This is the mid-season status on the habitat restoration monitoring for Carter and Sons. The work is on schedule. The restoration area that {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} established under its permit is being measured on the plan's method, and there is nothing on the engagement that needs your attention beyond this note.

The season is one part of the monitoring the permit requires, and it runs a few months end to end. This report covers where the work stands at the midpoint and what is left to do. It is a working report, not a finding on the site.
What we have done so far

The early monitoring visits are complete. Vegetation has been recorded along the fixed transects and in the sample plots, by species and cover. The gauges have been read on each visit, and the photo stations have been shot on their established headings.
Every observation is tied to its plot, its station, and the date. The field record is current and in the standard format. The data workbook is built and holds the results collected so far.

The hydrology readings are logged against their gauges and dates. The photo panels are filed by station, so this season's frames sit next to the earlier ones. Both are the kind of record a reviewer can open years out and follow without us.

The point of holding to one method is comparability. Each visit is run the same way, at the same stations, so the readings can be set against one another and against the seasons on either side. Where a visit shifted for the tide, the shift was logged so the record stays clean.

James Henderson has started the structure of the monitoring report. It is drafted from the checked data once the season's visits are in. Nothing has been characterized yet on partial data, which is deliberate.
What comes next

The remaining visits run on the same transects and by the same method as the completed ones. They are scheduled to the season's window and the tide, not to fixed dates, so each reading stays comparable with the last.

As results come in, they are entered and checked the same way, and the workbook is built out toward the full set. The totals are reconciled against the field record before anything leaves the office. The monitoring report is drafted last, once every visit is in and the totals have been verified.

Between now and delivery there is little that changes the shape of the work. The remaining visits are run, the readings are entered and checked, and the report is written from the full set. We hold to the plan's stations and method throughout, so the season reads as one record.
You will not have to chase us for status. If a reading or an observation looks like it needs your attention before the report, you will hear it from us when we see it, not at delivery.
Budget

This is a fixed-fee engagement of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}. It covers the field collection, the data workbook, the analysis, and the monitoring report. About half the fee is committed, which tracks with being about halfway through the work. I do not foresee anything in the remaining scope that would change the figure. If the site called for work beyond what was scoped, you would hear it from us before it was done.
Risks
The main variable is the weather and the tide. Either can move a visit by a day or two. We plan the visits around the water and keep enough margin that a short delay does not put the report at risk.

One item is worth flagging. A stand of an invasive species was noted along the upland edge, and we are tracking its extent against the earlier record. It does not change the plan for the season. We are recording it so the season's report reflects it.

Access to the far side of the area depends on the water, and a visit there can slip if the crossing is not reliable. We have raised it with your site contact and expect a standing arrangement for the field crew. It has not cost us a visit so far.
None of these rises to a concern today. We flag the ordinary ones so they are on the record and not a surprise later. If any of them changes, you will hear it from us when we see it.

The single next step is the next monitoring visit, run on the same transects and by the same method as the completed ones. After the season's visits are in and the totals are checked, James Henderson writes the monitoring report, and it goes out over the firm's signature. — William Schwartz
